name: Samoa
summary_text: Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, as recorded in the Human Dignity Trust country profile. The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it applies equally where one partner is transgender. A trans visitor in a same-sex relationship should treat Samoa as a jurisdiction where that conduct is a criminal offence carrying a custodial penalty.  The same statute removed the colonial-era offence of impersonating a woman, so no Samoan law targets gender expression itself. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that the new Crimes Act was in force that week and that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not at that time agitating for repeal of the sodomy provisions, so the decriminalisation position on that front remained unchanged.  Gender-diverse identity is culturally embedded in Samoa. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's stakeholder report for Samoa's Universal Periodic Review at the 39th session in 2021, titled 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa', describes the third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the stated aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation. That report is an advocacy submission rather than a source of binding protection, and the inventory does not establish any statutory mechanism for changing gender markers.

sources.title: Mental Health Act 2007 (Tulafono o le Tulaga Maloloina o le Mafaufau 2007)

sources.title: United Nations Human Rights Council - Universal Periodic Review (UPR) Working Group on Samoa, First and Second cycle (Third cycle due April-May 2021) and 2011 Joint Statement on SOGI
sources.documents: International human-rights review: First cycle Samoa rejected level 5 recommendations by Canada, France, Norway to repeal criminalization and investigate SOGI discrimination, accepted US recommendation to continue reconsideration; Second cycle accepted only Slovenia recommendation to reduce violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, rejected others on cultural sensitivity/Christian Constitution grounds; 2011 Samoa signed joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
sources.detail: UPR mechanism cited; third cycle due April and May 2021; 2011 joint statement title quoted; no URL visible

sources.title: Samoa Censorship Board bans - Milk (2009) and Rocketman (2019)
sources.documents: Documented enforcement/censorship incidents: 2009 ban on screening Milk about Harvey Milk while allowing Lesbian Vampire Killers same week; 2019 ban on Rocketman about Elton John; criticized as hypocritical/selective morality and protested by Samoa Fa'afafine Association.
sources.detail: Years 2009 and 2019 cited; Samoa Fa'afafine Association protest noted; no URL visible

name: Kosovo
summary_text: Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination extends that protection to gender identity. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both provisions remains inconsistent in practice, so the guarantees a visitor can cite are stronger than what is reliably delivered.  Legal gender recognition runs through the courts rather than an administrative procedure. In January 2019 Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on Kosovo identity documents was before the Constitutional Court of Kosovo, and applicants in Kosovo followed closely the European Court of Human Rights ruling in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, which held that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates private-life rights.  Partner recognition remains unadopted law. Parliament rejected a law recognising same-sex civil unions in March 2022. Prime Minister Albin Kurti pledged in April 2024 to legalise same-sex civil unions, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting the relevant bill, but as of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition that included the ruling party. IntelliNews reports that the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language would open the way to same-sex marriage if it enters into force.  Public LGBTI organising is visible in Prishtina, where the third annual Pride Parade was held alongside a week of exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The CSGD annual report for 2022 documented intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.

sources.title: Constitution of Kosovo
sources.documents: Bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation; cited as basis for LGBTQ protections and same-sex marriage debate; Article 144(3) requires Constitutional Court approval of amendments affecting civil rights
sources.detail: Cited as 'Constitution of Kosovo' promulgated 2008; Article 24 wording quoted verbatim in text; Article 144(3) referenced. No URL visible in provided text.

sources.title: Anti-Discrimination Law of 2004 (Ligji Kunder Diskriminimit / Zakon protiv diskriminacije) with 26 May 2015 amendments
sources.documents: Bans discrimination on basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, goods/services, housing etc; defines direct/indirect discrimination, harassment, victimization, segregation; 2015 amendments added gender identity, effective July 2015
sources.detail: Cited as 'Anti-Discrimination Law of 2004' passed by Kosovo Assembly; amendments approved 26 May 2015. No URL visible.
